seats: secular academic scholar of the Bible

fixes.why: The label quotes “raised” and “rise”, but three of the four examples read: united in His resurrection, power of His resurrection, the resurrection of the dead. Only Acts 2:24 shows “raised”. The row's 8 verses also repeat adjective rows 1 and 2 (Rom 6:4, 6:9, 2 Cor 1:9, Rev 20:6 recur there).
fixes.fix: Relabel “Death and the resurrection” with no quoted words, or merge the 8 verses into the adjective resurrection rows, which would take the hub to 24 rows. Keep the note's pointer to the verb rows.

fixes.row: “Not the God of the dead”, “Lord of the dead”; the dead judged (adjective)
fixes.why: One exchange is cut in two. Matt 22:31, Mark 12:25 and Luke 20:35 sit in the resurrection row; the next verses of the same Sadducee scene (the God of Abraham, not of the dead but of the living) sit under “the dead judged”. They are Jesus' argument from Exodus 3 for the living God, not a statement about judgment, so the row joins two unrelated themes and the passage cannot be read whole.
fixes.fix: Move Matt 22:32, Mark 12:26-27 and Luke 20:37-38 into “The resurrection of the dead; the dead raised”. Keep Rom 14:9 (“Lord of both the dead and the living”) and relabel the remainder “The dead judged; Lord of the dead”, or keep a small row “God of the living” with the three Gospel parallels beside Rom 14:9.

fixes.row: “Each will die for his own sin” (verb)
fixes.why: The note frames these verses as one side of the question “do the first man's guilt and death pass to all, or does each die for his own sin”. Ezek 18, Deut 24:16, Jer 31:30 and 2 Kgs 14:6 do not mention Adam. They speak of liability in courts and of the exile-era proverb about sour grapes. Setting them against Rom 5:12 reads a later doctrinal debate back into them.
fixes.fix: Reword the note: these verses answer who is held liable for a wrong (Deut 24:16; 2 Kgs 14:6) and the proverb that the children bear the fathers' sin (Ezek 18; Jer 31:30). Then: Rom 5:12 and 1 Cor 15:22 are in the next row; where traditions part on whether the first man's death passes to all, the page takes no side, and these verses are not about that question in their own setting. Keep Num 27:3.

fixes.row: Adam died; “as in Adam all die” (verb)
fixes.why: Answers the worker's question: Gen 5:5 is a fair verse for the label “Adam died”, but it comes last, after the two Pauline verses, so the Hebrew Scriptures are not heard first. Gen 5 repeats “and he died” for every name (Gen 5:8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 27, 31). Those verses are all in More, so Adam's line is singled out only because Paul names him. Gen 5:5 says only that Adam died at 930.
fixes.fix: List Gen 5:5 first. Add to the note: “Genesis 5 closes each name with ‘and he died’ (see More); Gen 5:5 says only that Adam died.”

fixes.row: Asleep: “not dead but asleep”, “rested with his fathers” (verb)
fixes.why: (1) The note says “The text uses sleep and rest of those who have died: the girl in Mark 5:39”. The verse has Jesus say the child is “not dead”, and the mourners laugh. The note settles an open point in the text. (2) The sleeping words are different original words: Greek katheudō (Mark 5:39), koimaō (John 11, 1 Thess 4) and Hebrew shakab “lay down” (2 Chr 16:13, which the Berean renders “rested”). The row shows each under the death word's tag, so a reader sees one vocabulary. (3) The row is 5 New Testament verses to 1 Old Testament verse.
fixes.fix: Rewrite the note: “Jesus says of the girl, ‘The child is not dead, but asleep’ (Mark 5:39; also Matt 9:24, Luke 8:52); of Lazarus the text says Jesus spoke of his death and the disciples took it as actual sleep (John 11:13); Paul writes of those ‘who have fallen asleep in Him’ (1 Thess 4:14). These are different Greek words, and the Hebrew in 2 Chr 16:13 is another, ‘lay down with his fathers’; the page does not make them one.” Keep the sentence that the page takes no side.

fixes.row: The law's penalty: “must surely be put to death”, “stone them to death” (verb)
fixes.why: Two faults. (1) Josh 1:18 is the tribes' pledge of obedience to Joshua and a commander's order, not a penalty of the law, so it is out of place. (2) 43 verses of capital statutes stand with no note. The same legal text sets limits that belong with them: two witnesses (Deut 17:6), no ransom for a murderer (Num 35:31), refuge for the manslayer (Num 35), no death for another's sin (Deut 24:16). Without these the row reads as a bare list of crimes, and the lead examples (killing, witnesses, the false prophet) differ in kind from Sabbath and sexual statutes in the same row.
fixes.fix: Move Josh 1:18 to the “Struck down” row or More. Add a note that the verses are statutes in the Covenant, Holiness and Deuteronomic collections, that the text itself sets limits (Deut 17:6; Num 35; Deut 24:16), and that the page does not say how often or whether they were carried out. Keep the label.

fixes.row: Buried, mourned, “gathered to his people”, full of years (verb)
fixes.why: Acts 21:13 is Paul saying he is ready “to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus”. No one is buried or mourned and no one has died; “weeping” is what put it in the row. Mark 5:39 and Luke 8:52 also appear in this row and in Asleep, and “not dead” fits neither well.
fixes.fix: Remove Acts 21:13 (it belongs to More, or to the Christ-died / dying-with-Christ rows). Optionally drop Mark 5:39 and Luke 8:52 from this row since Asleep carries them.

fixes.row: Struck down, killed, fallen by the sword (verb)
fixes.why: Prov 23:13 (“though you strike him with a rod, he will not die”) is a verse about discipline of a child that says no one is killed; it does not show the label and will read badly in a row of battles. 108 verses mix war, murder, assassination, statute, and the LORD's strikes (2 Kgs 19:35, 2 Sam 6:7, 1 Chr 13:10), which also sit in “The LORD brings death”. About 20 statute verses (Exod 21, Lev 24, Num 35) repeat “The law's penalty”, so the row cannot be told apart from it, and the row's own doors (instruction, judgment) point there.
fixes.fix: Remove Prov 23:13 to More. Add a note: “These verses tell of killing in war, in murder and manslaughter, in executions and in what the text says the LORD struck down. Statute verses appear again in The law's penalty; verses where the LORD is named appear again in The LORD brings death.” Consider leading with 1 Sam 17:50, 2 Kgs 25:21, Judg 9:54 and Heb 11:37 so the lead shows the range.

fixes.row: Worthy of death, sentenced to death (noun)
fixes.why: Several verses say the reverse: Pilate and Herod found nothing “deserving death” (Luke 23:15, 22), and Festus, Agrippa and Claudius Lysias found none in Paul (Acts 23:29, 25:25, 26:31, 28:18). The label says “worthy of death”, and the glancing reader will miss the negation. The row also puts Jesus' trial verses beside Deut 21:22 and 22:26, where the Gospels' account of His trial and the Hebrew law-court language meet; that is a real link, and only a note can say so.
fixes.fix: Relabel “Worthy of death, sentenced to death, or found not worthy”. Add a one-line note that the verses are verdicts and accusations in law courts, Hebrew and Roman, and that Jesus' and Paul's trials appear on both sides. Add “see also The death of Christ” for the Gospel trial verses.

fixes.why: 2 Tim 1:10 says Christ “has abolished death” and does not speak of His own death. It is already in “Death as ruler and enemy”. Heb 5:7 is a prayer to be saved from death and is also in “Delivered from death”. Both are in the note's list of what the death does by being in the row.
fixes.fix: Remove 2 Tim 1:10 from this row (keep it in the ruler row). Keep Heb 5:7 or move it to Delivered from death only; add “See also Christ died in the verb list and Jesus Christ raised from the dead in The dead” to the note.

fixes.row: Hub-wide: Christ's death and rising are split across three lists
fixes.why: The hub is cut by grammatical form, so the arc is cut apart: He died (verb row 5), His death (noun row 7), He was raised from the dead (adjective row 1), with Rom 6:9 and Rom 14:9 repeating across them. A reader gets the gospel's own sequence only by changing tabs. 25 rows is at the limit of 15-25.
fixes.fix: Keep the rows (they stand on different words), and add “See also” lines that name the other two rows in each of their notes. If rows must go, merge noun row 5 into adjective row 2.

fixes.row: The resurrection of the dead; the dead raised (adjective)
fixes.why: One row holds a dead person called back to this life (Luke 7:15, John 12:1, Matt 10:8, Heb 11:35) and the resurrection at the end (1 Cor 15:42, 1 Thess 4:16). The text itself marks the difference with “firstfruits”, “the first to rise”, “the last day”. Heb 11:35 looks back to Elijah's and Elisha's raisings in the Hebrew Scriptures. And no Hebrew Scripture verse stands in the resurrection rows at all, so the Old Testament looks silent on the question.
fixes.fix: Add to the note: “Some verses tell of someone raised to this life (Luke 7:15; John 12:1; Heb 11:35, which looks back to the widows' sons of Kings); others of the resurrection at the end (1 Cor 15; 1 Thess 4:16). The page keeps them in one row as the text uses one word.” Add Isa 26:19 and Dan 12:2 (see missing).

fixes.row: “Dead” said of the living: dead in sin, dead faith, dead works (adjective)
fixes.why: The note speaks only about James 2 and faith and works, but the heaviest verses here are Eph 2:1, 2:5 and Col 2:13, where traditions part on how far “dead in trespasses” means unable to respond. The label “dead in sin” is also worded as in one tradition's vocabulary. Jas 2:26 first uses “dead” of a literal body, as an analogy.
fixes.fix: Add to the note: “Where traditions part on what ‘dead in trespasses’ means for a person's ability to respond (Eph 2:1, 2:5; Col 2:13), the page takes no side.” Relabel “‘Dead’ said of people who are alive: in trespasses, faith without deeds, dead works”, and note that Jas 2:26 compares to a body without a spirit.

fixes.row: What the text says follows dying, side by side (verb)
fixes.why: The row is fair in its mix, but the verses are speeches inside books: Qoheleth reasoning “under the sun” (Eccl 9), Job in complaint (Job 14), David at his son's death. The text itself says Job's friends did not speak rightly (Job 42:7), and the speaker is not the book's last word. A reader who sees them bare takes them as flat statements. Also the lead four are Eccl 9:5, Job 14:14, 2 Sam 12:23, Phil 1:21; “the dead know nothing” comes first and is seen first.
fixes.fix: Add to the note one sentence: “Eccl 9, Job 14 and 2 Sam 12 are the words of Qoheleth, Job and David in their own books.” Order the row in the Bible's order so no reading leads (Job 14:10, 14; 2 Sam 12:23; Eccl 9:4-5; Luke 16:22; John 11:25-26; Rom 14:8; Phil 1:21; Heb 9:27; Rev 14:13).

fixes.row: The LORD brings death and gives life (verb)
fixes.why: Of 12 verses only 1 Sam 2:6 and Deut 32:39 carry “gives life”. The other ten are judgments. The text supplies its own counterweight, Ezek 33:11 (“I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked”) and Ezek 18:23, which sit in other rows. A reader who sees only this row gets a one-sided view of the LORD's relation to death, and the label says life as well.
fixes.fix: Add a see-also to the note: “Ezek 33:11 and 18:23, where the LORD says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, are under The death of the wicked, of the righteous, of His saints.”

fixes.why: The row's doors include the card named Sheol (id hell). Rev 20:14 casts Death and Hades into the lake of fire, but a door labelled with a Hebrew word that does not occur in these four verses points a reader from a Revelation phrase to the Hebrew Sheol. The note correctly says Sheol and Hades are different words, so the door contradicts it.
fixes.fix: Replace the door on this row with judgment alone, or rename the door to the card's own title if it is shown to the reader as “Hades”. Do not link the second death to Sheol.

worker_points.point: 1. Noun row 1 and verb rows 3 and 4: sin, guilt and death, set side by side
worker_points.why: The Ezek 18, Deut 24:16, Jer 31:30 verses are not about Adam; the note should say so (see verb row 3 fix). Gen 5:5 should come first in the Adam row. The row-1 lead four (Rom 6:23, 5:12, Jas 1:15, 1 Cor 15:56) are all New Testament; Deut 21:22 or Prov 13:14 could come first so the Hebrew Scriptures lead. Acts 23:29 (no charge worthy of death) is a law-court verse, not about sin, and is also in Worthy of death.

worker_points.point: Is “Adam died; as in Adam all die” fair for Gen 5:5 beside 1 Cor 15:22 and Rom 5:15?
worker_points.why: The label is fair as a description of the two Pauline verses, and Gen 5:5 does say Adam died. But Gen 5:5 is last in the row, and the refrain of Gen 5 is lost. List Gen 5:5 first and add the sentence about Gen 5 in the note.

worker_points.point: 2. Verb row 2 “You will surely die”, with Gen 3:4 inside
worker_points.why: The same Hebrew phrase appears in the king's and priest's mouths (1 Sam 14:44, 22:16; 1 Kgs 2:37, 42; Gen 20:7), and the row shows that Gen 2:17 uses a courtroom formula, which is a text fact and not a reading. The note flags Gen 3:3 as report and 3:4 as denial. Not shown but fair: Gen 3:19 and the tree of life (see missing).
The label is the text's own phrase and all four examples show it. The note takes no side. Only the door to Sheol needs removing.

worker_points.point: 4. Noun row 4 Death beside Sheol, Hades, the grave, the pit
worker_points.why: Ps 18:5, Ps 49:14 and Hos 13:14 lead, so the Hebrew Scriptures come first, and the note says Sheol and Hades are different words. The row uses “beside”, which equates nothing. 2 Chr 32:33 (buried in the upper tombs; paid honor at his death) is a burial verse, a weak fit for Sheol, but the label says “the grave”.
The note on Rev 20 and 1 Pet 4:6 is neutral. The faults are the quoted label in noun row 5, the split of Matt 22:32 from Matt 22:31, and no Hebrew Scripture verse in any resurrection row.

worker_points.point: 6. Verb row 7: one neutral label; lead order; Luke 16:22 placement
worker_points.why: One neutral label is better than two quoted ones. The lead order puts the unconscious reading first and the fix is canon order. Luke 16:22 fits because it contains “died”; Luke 16:23 is Hades and is rightly left out. Add the sentence on the speakers.

worker_points.point: 7. Noun row 6 end of death done and still to come
worker_points.why: 2 Tim 1:10, 1 Cor 15:26 and Rev 21:4 are set side by side and the note says how they fit is read differently. Isa 25:8 is the Hebrew Scriptures' own verse in the row. Hos 13:14 is quoted at 1 Cor 15:55 and appears in three rows; harmless.

worker_points.point: 8. Death of Christ and Christ died: what the death does; Lord's Supper; Heb 9:15
worker_points.why: The note is neutral on mechanism. Remove 2 Tim 1:10 from the noun row; cross-reference the two rows; “communes” in the note is an unclear word, use “unites us to Him”.
The note is neutral. Add a see-also that other words (synapothnēskō in 2 Tim 2:11, apogenomenos in 1 Pet 2:24, nekroō in Col 3:5) carry the same theme and are under Other words.
The faith-and-works note is neutral, but the larger debate in the row is Eph 2:1 and Col 2:13 and has no note.

worker_points.point: 11. LORD brings death; the law's penalty (hard verses; rabbi and young African American believer to judge framing)
worker_points.why: Not a doctrine row, and each LORD verse names the LORD. The law's penalty row needs a note giving the limits that the text itself sets and omits Josh 1:18; that is a scholarly point about the label meeting its verses, and the other two seats will judge framing.

worker_points.point: 12. Noun row 9 sets verdicts against Jesus, Paul and the law side by side
worker_points.why: Fair idea, but the negations (found not worthy) need to show in the label.

Rows naming the LORD, Christ, Jesus or the Son of Man are picks of verses that name Him; verses with only “He” or “Him” are in More. Rom 8:11 (the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus) sits in adjective row 1 and is named by hand; fine. Rev 6:8 is Death and Hades as riders, not a person claim.

missing.what: The Hebrew Scriptures' own hope of rising, absent from every resurrection row. Isa 26:19 (“Your dead will live”) is reachable only under the shades in Other words, and Dan 12:2 (many who sleep in the dust will awake) has no death word. Job 19:25-26 and Hos 6:2 likewise. As built, the hub has the Old Testament silent on resurrection, which it is not.

The Eden story's own arc past the sentence: the return to dust and the barred way to the tree of life, which show what the sentence meant in the narrative. They contain no death word, so the builder did not reach them; a note or see-also on the “You will surely die” row would let the story's arc show.

The Hebrew Scriptures' death-free end of the story: the tree of life and the promise of no more death in Rev 22 and Isa 65:20, 66:24 mirror Gen 2-3. Only Isa 25:8 and Rev 21:4 are in the hub, and Rev 22:2-3 (no longer any curse; tree of life) is not. A see-also from the ruler-and-enemy row to the tree of life would close the arc.

examples_checked: 22 of 25 rows' examples show their label. Noun “raised, rise” fails (3 of 4 show only “resurrection”); “Worthy of death” shows the negation in some verses; “Not the God of the dead” shows its first quote in 1 of 4 examples (Matt 22:32) while the others show the judged-dead half. Misfits found: Acts 21:13, Josh 1:18, Prov 23:13, 2 Tim 1:10.
summary: The hub is built with care, keeps its no-side notes where traditions part, and its Hebrew Scripture rows are honest, but it needs a handful of fixes: one label quoting words its verses lack, a Gospel scene cut in two, a note setting Ezekiel 18 and Deuteronomy 24 against Adam, and the Hebrew hope of resurrection missing. Four verses sit in the wrong row and three notes need a line so that a reader sees the speakers, the text's own limits and the other words involved.
